# Notes on 2 Chronicles 36

**About these notes:** I ran out of search and page-read allowances before covering everything. I read the full Enduring Word (Guzik) and Ellicott pages, but the Ellicott page cut off partway through v. 10. For the rest I used Bible Hub, StudyLight, Precept Austin, Blue Letter Bible, Got Questions, Bible Odyssey and New Advent/Catholic.com. I didn't find, and so have left out:
- Pages from Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan or Pentecostal-denominational sites, or Spurgeon
- NET Bible notes
- Orthodox readings
- Any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview (vv. 1–23)**
- Guzik says all four of the last kings rejected God and His prophets. God warned them again and again, with compassion, but they mocked the warnings until there was no remedy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/
- Matthew Henry says the ruin came "by degrees." God arranged it that way to give the people time and reason to repent. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_036.cfm
- Constable says the writer measures each king against David to show that none of David's descendants matched him. So the promised Son of David was still to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-36.html

**v. 1**
- JFB: the people crowned Shallum (Jehoahaz) instead of his older brother Eliakim, from whom they expected little good. His anointing (2 Kings 23:30) was probably meant to strengthen what was a popular election. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/36-1.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the wording may show the nation's eagerness for this son, who was not the eldest. Elsewhere he is called Shallum (1 Chr 3:15; Jer 22:10–12). Same URL.
- Guzik quotes Knapp: Jehoahaz was "the preference of the multitude, not the appointment of God." Knapp adds that leaving him out of Matthew 1 may mean God did not count him a true successor. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: Kings gives the same age and adds his mother's name. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/36.htm
- Guzik: 2 Kings 23:32 says he did evil. Josiah's reforms did not last. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**v. 3**
- Clarke: Necho treated Judah as conquered and paying tribute. He removed Jehoahaz because the people had crowned him without Necho's consent, perhaps just to show who was in charge. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-chronicles-36.html
- Ellicott: "put him down" really means "removed him" from reigning. The levy was a fine. Riblah was on the Orontes River in Syria. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/36.htm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: 2 Kings adds that Jehoahaz died in Egypt (compare Jer 22:10–12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/36.htm
- Coffman: Necho was now master of Judah, and God's people were "merely vassals of Egypt." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-chronicles-36.html
- Guzik: Jehoiakim was a puppet king, and Judah became Egypt's buffer against Babylon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**v. 5**
- Guzik, quoting Clarke and Wiseman: Jehoiakim taxed the people heavily to pay Egypt, while building himself a palace with forced labour (Jer 22:13–19). He also burned Jeremiah's scroll (Jer 36), and Trapp adds that he killed the prophet Urijah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**v. 6**
- Guzik dates this to 605 BC, the first of three invasions (605, 597, 587/586). He says the Babylonian Chronicles record it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/
- **The apparent conflict with Jeremiah.** Jeremiah 22:19 says Jehoiakim would be buried in disgrace outside Jerusalem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/ Three answers:
  - Knapp (quoted by Guzik): the verse says he was bound *to be* taken to Babylon, not that he got there. He may have been released after promising to submit. Same URL.
  - Ellicott: likewise, the text doesn't say the plan was carried out. He thinks Nebuchadnezzar humiliated Jehoiakim and left him as a vassal king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/36.htm
  - The Expositor's Bible (an older critical-leaning commentary) reads it differently. It suggests the Chronicler left out "slept with his fathers" and added the chains to avoid a puzzle: why the wicked Jehoiakim would die peacefully when the godly Josiah died in battle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/2_chronicles/36.htm
- Clarke: Archbishop Ussher counted Jeremiah's seventy years from this point. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-chronicles-36.html

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: this is not in Kings but is confirmed by Daniel 1:2. "His temple" was the temple of Bel-Merodach (Marduk). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/36.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: "abominations" probably means idolatry and tyranny, such as greed and shedding innocent blood. "That which was found in him" means his general character and conduct. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/36.htm
- Guzik: his rebellion against Babylon (2 Kings 24:1–7) was among the things "found against him." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**v. 9**
- Some older translations read "eight years old" here. Ellicott and Guzik both say "eighteen" is correct, as in 2 Kings 24:8 and some manuscripts and ancient versions. The difference is a single small Hebrew letter (yod, which stands for ten). Ellicott adds that Ezekiel's description of him couldn't fit an eight-year-old. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/36.htm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/
- Guzik, quoting Knapp: Jeremiah 36:30 ("none to sit on the throne of David") means no one would sit *firmly*. A three-month reign doesn't count. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: "the return of the year" means spring, the season when kings went to war. Some temple vessels had already been taken (v. 7). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/36.htm
- Guzik, quoting Wiseman: Babylonian ration tablets name "Yaukin king of the Judeans." Guzik, quoting Dilday, also says Jerusalem fell in stages, including the surrender on 16 March 597 BC. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**vv. 11–12**
- Matthew Henry: the king should have humbled himself before a "poor prophet." Because he would not serve God, he was made a slave to his enemies. "God will find some way or other to humble those that will not humble themselves." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_036.cfm
- Guzik, quoting Payne: Zedekiah ignored Jeremiah, later asked him questions, and finally begged for help, but he never truly submitted. Guzik notes the name Zedekiah means "the LORD is righteous." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**v. 13**
- Precept Austin: Zedekiah broke his oath to the king of Babylon (Ezek 17:18), which sped up the nation's fall. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary
- Coffman: the final destruction probably wouldn't have happened if Zedekiah had kept his sacred oath. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-chronicles-36.html
- Guzik: Zedekiah believed false prophets who promised victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**v. 14**
- Matthew Henry: idolatry was the great sin, and the chief priests, who should have opposed it, were the "ring-leaders." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/36-21.html
- Duguid (in Precept Austin): the disobedience was widespread, and the Chronicler piles up strong words toward a climax. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary

**v. 15**
- Matthew Henry: God "rises betimes" (early) because His prophets were diligent. The harder ministers work, the more people will have to answer for if it is in vain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_036.cfm
- Henry (Concise): God calls sinners back through His word, ministers, conscience and providence, which shows His unwillingness that any should perish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/36-1.htm

**v. 16**
- Matthew Henry: the wrath came "without remedy, for it was sinning against the remedy." God takes abuse of His messengers as done to Himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_036.cfm
- Clarke: after long patience, God's mercy gave them up because their case was hopeless. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-chronicles-36.html
- Precept Austin: God's long-restrained patience finally gave way to just judgment on His own covenant people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary

**v. 17**
- Matthew Henry: they rejected the God who had compassion on them, so they were handed to men who had none. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_036.cfm
- Steven Cole (in Precept Austin): when God judges a nation, the godly suffer alongside the ungodly. God showed compassion before the judgment, but the Babylonians showed none. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary

**vv. 17–19**
- A commentator quoted by Guzik: "all, every" appears five times in these verses, stressing that there was no escape. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/

**v. 18**
- Guzik (on Ezra 1): these treasures are the ones Cyrus later sent back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-1/

**v. 19**
- Precept Austin: everything Judah trusted in was burned, which shows God's presence is not tied to a building. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary
- Constable: the temple's burning symbolized the end of God's glory among His people in the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/36-21.html

**v. 20**
- Matthew Henry: the survivors were made poor and enslaved, ruled by people who hated them for as long as that empire lasted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/36-21.html

**v. 21**
- Expositor's Bible: this rests on Leviticus 25:1–7, the command to leave the land unplanted every seventh year. Seventy years of exile would make up for 490 years in which those Sabbath years were not kept. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/2_chronicles/36.htm
- Barnes: there had been about seventy broken Sabbath years. He adds that "seventy" may be a round number for a desolation of about 68 years. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brv/2-chronicles/36-21.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: the link between Jeremiah's prophecy and the law is theological, not an exact year-count. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/36-21.html
- Matthew Henry: if they refused to let the land rest, God would make it rest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/36-1.htm
- Andrew Hill (in Precept Austin): the Chronicler gives two reasons for the exile: rejecting the prophets (v. 16) and failing to give the land its Sabbath rest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary

**v. 22**
- Constable: the book ends not with human failure but with God's faithfulness. God controlled Persia's king just as He had controlled the others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-36.html
- Dillard (in Precept Austin): a new exodus is at hand, this time by moving a Persian king's heart rather than forcing a reluctant Pharaoh. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary
- Guzik: God gave Cyrus urgency, so the release came in his first year, 538 BC. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-36/
- Coffman: Isaiah had named Cyrus generations before he was born. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/2-chronicles-36.html
- Pulpit Commentary sermon notes: ancient inscriptions show Cyrus worshipped many gods and credited Merodach (Marduk). The biblical writer says the true source of his impulse was the LORD. https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_chronicles/36-23.htm
- Barnes: these verses are repeated at the start of Ezra, and Chronicles and Ezra were probably once one work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/36-22.htm
- Clarke: some think these two verses were copied into Chronicles from Ezra by mistake, so the book properly ends at v. 21. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-chronicles-36.html

**v. 23**
- Selman (in Precept Austin): "to build Him a house" deliberately echoes the Davidic covenant. In the Chronicler's mind, it points to both houses: the temple and David's royal line. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary
- Mabie (same page): whatever Cyrus himself believed, the LORD was using him to carry out His plan. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary
- Matthew Henry: God's church may be cast down but is not cast off. His people stay in the furnace only until the impurities are removed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_036.cfm

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no page showing a real disagreement between Protestant traditions on this chapter. The teachers I read, Reformed, Baptist, Calvary Chapel (Guzik and Smith) and Methodist (Clarke), all read it much the same way. Two differences of emphasis:

- **v. 23, the future hope.** Constable stresses a future for Israel as a nation under a perfect Davidic Son. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-36.html Bible Hub's study note instead links Cyrus as an "anointed" deliverer to Christ freeing His people from a deeper captivity. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_God_choose_Cyrus_in_2_Chronicles.htm
- **vv. 15–16, application to nations.** Chuck Smith applies the passage to America as a nation that has forsaken God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/36-22.html This is a preacher's application, not a doctrinal dispute.

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- v. 1: One scholar quoted on Precept Austin notes the Chronicler gives no moral verdict on Jehoahaz, unlike 2 Kings 23:32. By letting the kingship simply fade away, he leaves room for the restored kingship that Jeremiah and Ezekiel predicted. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary
- v. 23: Konkel (same page) contrasts the two endings. Kings ends with Jehoiachin still in exile and no promise of restoration. Chronicles answers the exile with a new era. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-36-commentary
- vv. 22–23: Bible Odyssey says the Cyrus Cylinder is often cited as outside evidence for the decree. A recent rereading, though, shows it concerns returning divine images to cities around Babylon. The return to Judah was a long process in waves. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/babylonian-exile/ The Cylinder says Cyrus restored worship with the help of Marduk. https://2fwww.bibleodyssey.org/people/related-articles/cyrus-the-messiah/
- Got Questions, by contrast, suggests Daniel may have shown Cyrus the prophecies about him, citing Josephus. https://www.gotquestions.org/Cyrus-Bible.html

**Catholic**
- Whole book: the Catholic Encyclopedia says the author's interest is the temple and its worship. He wanted to show that kings and people prospered or suffered depending on their faithfulness to that worship. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/paralipomenon-the-books-of It says the books were written after the return, since they quote the decree of Cyrus. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11472a.htm
- v. 13: the Catholic Encyclopedia calls Nebuchadnezzar fairly lenient. It says Zedekiah's ingratitude was "particularly odious," and he would have been treated more gently had he been less stubborn (Jer 38:17–18). https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/10666c.htm
